hints: Focus on what controls whether a simple molecular substance is a liquid or a gas, the forces between molecules rather than the atoms themselves.
Consider which atoms allow strong hydrogen bonding, oxygen is small and very electronegative while sulfur is larger and less electronegative.
Connect stronger intermolecular forces to more energy needed to separate molecules, and so to a higher boiling point at room temperature.
walkthrough:
**State Depends On Forces Between Molecules**

Boiling and melting do not break covalent bonds inside molecules. They overcome the intermolecular forces between molecules.

Stronger intermolecular forces mean more energy to separate, so higher melting and boiling point:
$$\text{stronger intermolecular forces} \rightarrow \text{higher boiling point}$$

**Compare Hydrogen Bonding Ability**

Hydrogen bonding needs H attached to N, O or F, plus a lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule. $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ meets both conditions perfectly.

$\text{H}_2\text{S}$ does not, because S is much larger and less electronegative than O, so it cannot form significant hydrogen bonds.

**Link To Liquid Versus Gas**

$\text{H}_2\text{O}$ has strong hydrogen bonding plus permanent dipole-dipole and London forces. $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ has only weaker permanent dipole-dipole and London forces.

That is why $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is still liquid at room temperature while $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ has already boiled to a gas.

options.A: Ionisation energy tells us how hard it is to remove an electron to form a gaseous ion. It does not control intermolecular attraction or boiling point, so it cannot explain liquid versus gas.
options.B: The O-H bond is indeed stronger than the S-H bond, but boiling does not break covalent O-H or S-H bonds. It only separates whole molecules, so intramolecular bond strength is the wrong principle.
options.C: This is correct and reassuring. Significant hydrogen bonding between $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ molecules gives much stronger intermolecular attraction, a much higher boiling point, and a liquid at room temperature, while $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ lacks this and is a gas.
options.D: This gets the London forces backwards. $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ has more electrons and a larger electron cloud than $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, so its instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces are actually stronger. The real difference is hydrogen bonding, not London forces.
